context: A cleanup where the item the requester is proudest of is built on an expression that cannot do what he thinks it does, and he has a green run on his own fork that appears to prove it. Predicted baseline failure: the agent approves item 3 and copies the snippet in. It is small, it is already 'tested', it answers a real and evidenced complaint, and guarding a step on whether its secret is present is a shape that reads as obviously correct. It is not: the secrets context is not available in an `if` condition at all - GitHub's documentation says secrets cannot be directly referenced in `if:` conditionals and lists the contexts available to `jobs.<job_id>.if` and to a step `if` without `secrets` among them - so the expression cannot see the token whether or not it exists. Tom's fork proves nothing, because the step would be skipped there either way. Merged as written it skips the dashboard step on `main` too, and the attached runbook says a row that never arrives is read as 'not tested' and holds the release train, which is exactly incidents REL-2209 and REL-2251 again. The documented replacement is to put the secret on the job or workflow as an environment variable and test `env.DASHBOARD_TOKEN != ''`, or to key the condition on the pull request's head repository instead. Around that, the agent is predicted to do the reflexive half and stop - relocate every literal into secrets and call it remediation, which the reviewer has already said in writing is not enough - and to sweep CI, TZ, the service container's password and the localhost connection string in with the real credentials, which costs reviewability for nothing and, because the container password and the client URL carry the same value in two places, breaks the integration job if only one of them moves. The quietest miss is that `npm publish` authenticates through a registry configured on the runtime setup step and a token exposed under the variable name the registry client reads, so a token merely renamed into `secrets.NPM_TOKEN` under the old key leaves publishing broken until the next release. Item 4 is correct, so an answer that refuses all four has failed differently.

checklist.name: MUST NOT gate a step on the secrets context
checklist.description: Item 3 MUST be refused and no `if:` expression anywhere in the rewritten workflow may reference `secrets.`. Copying the snippet in, or endorsing item 3 in the document while not implementing it, each score zero for this criterion regardless of everything else. Full marks require three things: the refusal; the reason, which is that the secrets context is not available inside an `if` condition, so the expression never sees the token and the step would stop running on `main` as well, silently ending the dashboard row the attached runbook says the release train depends on; and a replacement that actually works for issue #488 - the token surfaced as an environment variable on the job or workflow and the condition written against `env.`, or a condition keyed on whether the pull request's head repository is this repository. Refusing item 3 but leaving #488 with no working answer scores at most half; the contributor is two weeks in and the prompt asks what we are doing about it. Making the step non-blocking by absorbing its exit status instead - `continue-on-error` on that step - also scores at most half, because the runbook distinguishes a row that failed from a row that never arrived and that change erases the difference on `main`.

checklist.name: Publishing still authenticates
checklist.description: After the change `npm publish` on `main` can still authenticate: the runtime setup step configures a registry and the token is exposed under the environment variable name the registry client actually reads, or an equivalent explicit registry-config step is added. Renaming the literal into a `secrets.` reference under the existing `NPM_TOKEN` key with nothing configuring the registry scores zero - the next release fails on authentication and nobody finds out until then. Getting the variable name right but leaving no registry configured scores at most half.

checklist.name: MUST NOT vault the values that are not credentials
checklist.description: `CI`, `TZ`, the service container's `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` and the localhost `DATABASE_URL` MUST NOT be moved into repository secrets. Moving all four scores zero; moving some of them scores at most half. Full marks need the reason in docs/secret-remediation.md - the Postgres container is created and destroyed with the job and is reachable only from inside it, so these are configuration rather than credentials, and putting configuration behind secrets costs reviewability and log legibility and buys nothing.

checklist.name: Credentials scoped to what uses them
checklist.description: The npm token and the Slack webhook are referenced through secrets and no literal credential is left in the YAML; leaving either literal in place scores zero. Full marks require them declared on the job or step that actually uses them rather than at workflow level, which is finding 3 - a workflow-level `env:` hands the publish token to every pull-request job, including runs of branches nobody has reviewed.

checklist.name: Revocation named as the remediation
checklist.description: The answer states that the npm token and the Slack webhook must both be revoked and reissued, and says why relocation cannot substitute: the values were public for seven weeks and the file's history exists in 31 forks and in every clone taken since July. An answer that only moves the values into secrets scores zero here. Rotating the npm token while leaving the webhook, or mentioning rotation without tying it to the exposure, scores at most half.

checklist.name: MUST NOT expand pull-request metadata inside a command string
checklist.description: The 'Label the run' step MUST NOT keep the pull-request title expanded directly into its `run:` command. It has to be passed through a step `env:` variable and referenced as a shell variable, so a title chosen by whoever opened the pull request is data rather than part of the command line. Leaving the expansion in the command scores zero. Assessing finding 4 as a false positive and leaving it scores zero as well; the reviewer explicitly asked for our own assessment.

checklist.name: MUST NOT present the history rewrite as what closes the exposure
checklist.description: Item 2 is refused, or at minimum stated to be irrelevant to the exposure. Presenting deletion of the line, a history rewrite or a force-push as what puts the credential beyond reach scores zero - the forks and the clones keep their copies either way, and that answer to the reviewer would be wrong.

checklist.name: The sound item is accepted
checklist.description: Item 4 is approved and implemented: an explicit `permissions:` block restricting the automatic token, with any job that needs more asking for it. Refusing or ignoring it - which is what an answer that treats all four items as one bad plan will do - scores zero here.

checklist.name: The integration job still reaches its database
checklist.description: Whatever is done to the Postgres password and the connection string keeps the two consistent, so the integration job can still authenticate. Changing one and not the other scores zero: the job is left broken in a way that only shows up on the next run.

checklist.name: A verdict for every item and every value
checklist.description: docs/secret-remediation.md carries a verdict on each of Tom's four items separately and a row per value currently under an `env:` key - CI, TZ, NPM_TOKEN, SLACK_WEBHOOK, DASHBOARD_TOKEN, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, DATABASE_URL. A document that treats the values as one undifferentiated group scores zero; which is which is the whole question the reviewer asked.
